tools.name: mcp__gmail__draft_gmail_message
tools.description:
Creates a draft email in the user's Gmail account. Supports new, reply, and forward
drafts with optional attachments. Supports Gmail's "Send As" feature to draft from
configured alias addresses.

To save a forward as a draft for review, pass forward_message_id. The original
subject, body (quoted with a "Forwarded message" header), and attachments are
carried over. In forward mode, body (if any) is prepended as a note, subject is
optional, and threading, reply, and signature options do not apply.

SCHEDULED SEND IS NOT AVAILABLE. Gmail's REST API exposes no send-time
parameter; the Schedule send feature is web-UI only, and a message cannot be
placed in the Scheduled folder through the API. Do not claim a message was
scheduled. To deliver at a chosen time, create a draft with
draft_gmail_message. An external scheduler must retain the message data to
create and send a new message via send_gmail_message then, or call
users.drafts.send with the draft ID returned by draft_gmail_message.
Alternatively, let the user schedule the draft in the Gmail UI.

schema.name: mcp__gmail__draft_gmail_message
schema.description:
Creates a draft email in the user's Gmail account. Supports new, reply, and forward
drafts with optional attachments. Supports Gmail's "Send As" feature to draft from
configured alias addresses.

To save a forward as a draft for review, pass forward_message_id. The original
subject, body (quoted with a "Forwarded message" header), and attachments are
carried over. In forward mode, body (if any) is prepended as a note, subject is
optional, and threading, reply, and signature options do not apply.

SCHEDULED SEND IS NOT AVAILABLE. Gmail's REST API exposes no send-time
parameter; the Schedule send feature is web-UI only, and a message cannot be
placed in the Scheduled folder through the API. Do not claim a message was
scheduled. To deliver at a chosen time, create a draft with
draft_gmail_message. An external scheduler must retain the message data to
create and send a new message via send_gmail_message then, or call
users.drafts.send with the draft ID returned by draft_gmail_message.
Alternatively, let the user schedule the draft in the Gmail UI.

user_google_email.description: The user's Google email address. Required for authentication.

subject.description: Email subject. Required unless forwarding (then defaults to 'Fwd: <original subject>').

body.description: Email body. Required unless forwarding, where it becomes an optional note prepended above the quoted original.

body_format.description: Email body format. Use 'plain' for plaintext or 'html' for HTML content.

forward_message_id.description: Set to a Gmail message ID to save a forward of that message as a draft for review. The original subject, body, and (optionally) attachments are carried over; 'body' becomes an optional note prepended to the forward.

include_forwarded_attachments.description: When forwarding, whether to include the original message's attachments. Ignored unless forward_message_id is set.

from_name.description: Optional sender display name (e.g., 'Peter Hartree'). If provided, the From header will be formatted as 'Name <email>'.

from_email.description: Optional 'Send As' alias email address. Must be configured in Gmail settings (Settings > Accounts > Send mail as). If not provided, uses the account's default Send As address, falling back to the authenticated user's email when Gmail returns no usable Send-As entry or settings access is not authorized.

thread_id.description: Optional Gmail thread ID to reply within. When in_reply_to is omitted, replies to the latest non-draft, non-trash message with an RFC Message-ID.

in_reply_to.description: Optional RFC Message-ID to explicitly reply to a specific message (e.g., '<message123@gmail.com>'). Omit to reply to the latest eligible message in thread_id.

references.description: Optional Message-ID ancestry chain. Normally omit when thread_id is provided; the server derives the chain through the selected reply target.

attachments.description: Optional list of attachments. Each can have: 'url' (fetch from URL — works with MCP attachment URLs from get_drive_file_download_url / get_gmail_attachment_content), OR 'path' (file path, auto-encodes), OR 'content' (standard base64, not urlsafe) + 'filename'. Optional 'mime_type'. Optional 'content_id' (string) makes the attachment inline-rendered: it lands in a multipart/related part with `Content-ID: ` and `Content-Disposition: inline`, and the HTML body can reference it via `` (RFC 2392). Without `content_id` the attachment is a regular multipart/mixed attachment.

include_signature.description: Whether to append the Gmail signature from Settings > Signature when available. Defaults to true.

quote_original.description: Whether to include the original message as a quoted reply. Only has an effect when thread_id is provided. Defaults to false.

schema.name: mcp__gmail__get_gmail_attachment_content
schema.description:
Downloads an email attachment and saves it to local disk.

In HTTP mode, returns a temporary download URL (valid for 1 hour).
May re-fetch message metadata to resolve filename and MIME type.

message_id.description: The ID of the Gmail message containing the attachment.

attachment_id.description: The ID of the attachment to download.

user_google_email.description: The user's Google email address. Required.

return_base64.description:
When True, includes the full attachment as a
standard base64 string in the response (in addition to any file
path or download URL). Useful for sandboxed clients that cannot
reach localhost download URLs or the MCP server's local file
paths (e.g. containerized agents with network allowlists). The
returned base64 uses the standard alphabet, so it can be passed
directly to tools like ``draft_gmail_message`` that expect

attachment_index.description:
Zero-based attachment position from
the message-content response. Lets the server resolve Gmail's
refreshed attachment IDs against current metadata before every
download, selecting the current attachment ID, filename and MIME type.

tools.name: mcp__gmail__get_gmail_message_content
tools.description:
Retrieves the full content (subject, sender, recipients, body) of a specific Gmail message.

Bodies are returned inline and truncated at 20,000 characters. Set full=True to
get the complete, untruncated message instead: it is exported to storage and the
response carries a short-lived download URL (HTTP transport) or file path (stdio
transport) rather than the body, so large messages never stream through the model
context. Stateless deployments without GCS staging have no storage, so there
full=True returns the untruncated body inline; with GCS staging configured it
returns a signed download URL like any other HTTP deployment.

tools.name: mcp__gmail__manage_gmail_filter
tools.description:
Manages Gmail filters: create, delete, update, and apply to existing mail.

- update: Gmail has no filter update API, so the filter is recreated (new
  one first, then the old one is deleted) and its ID changes. A passed
  criteria or filter_action replaces that whole object; omit one to keep
  the old filter's.
- apply: runs a filter's label actions on mail ALREADY in the mailbox
  (Gmail filters only act on new mail). Only matching messages change,
  not whole conversations as in the web UI. Use filter_id, or criteria +
  filter_action for an ad-hoc run. Forwarding is never applied. Use
  dry_run=true first to see the search query and the match count.
  Needs the gmail.modify scope in addition to gmail.settings.basic.

tools.name: mcp__gmail__send_gmail_message
tools.description:
Sends an email using the user's Gmail account. Supports new emails, replies, and
forwards, with optional attachments. Supports Gmail's "Send As" feature to send
from configured alias addresses.

To forward an existing message, pass forward_message_id. The original subject,
body (quoted with a "Forwarded message" header), and attachments are carried over.
In forward mode, body (if any) is prepended as a note and subject is optional.
Threading, reply, and signature options do not apply when forwarding.

THIS TOOL SENDS IMMEDIATELY AND CANNOT SCHEDULE. Gmail's REST API exposes no
send-time parameter; Schedule send is a web-UI feature with no API equivalent,
so no argument to this tool can defer delivery. Never tell a user a message
was scheduled. For "prepare now, deliver later", create a draft with
draft_gmail_message. An external scheduler must retain the message data to
create and send a new message via send_gmail_message at the chosen time, or
call users.drafts.send with the draft ID returned by draft_gmail_message.
Alternatively, let the user schedule that draft in the Gmail UI.

schema.description:
Sends an email using the user's Gmail account. Supports new emails, replies, and

body (quoted with a "Forwarded message" header), and attachments are carried over.
In forward mode, body (if any) is prepended as a note and subject is optional.
Threading, reply, and signature options do not apply when forwarding.

THIS TOOL SENDS IMMEDIATELY AND CANNOT SCHEDULE. Gmail's REST API exposes no
send-time parameter; Schedule send is a web-UI feature with no API equivalent,
so no argument to this tool can defer delivery. Never tell a user a message
was scheduled. For "prepare now, deliver later", create a draft with
draft_gmail_message. An external scheduler must retain the message data to
create and send a new message via send_gmail_message at the chosen time, or
call users.drafts.send with the draft ID returned by draft_gmail_message.
Alternatively, let the user schedule that draft in the Gmail UI.

user_google_email.description: The user's Google email address. Required for authentication.

to.description: Recipient email address. Optional when replying with reply_all=True, which derives it from the thread.

subject.description: Email subject. Required when sending; optional when forwarding (defaults to 'Fwd: <original subject>').

body.description: Email body content (plain text or HTML). Required when sending. When forwarding, this is an optional note prepended above the quoted original.

body_format.description: Format of the body content (and of the prepended note when forwarding). Use 'plain' for plaintext or 'html' for HTML content.

forward_message_id.description: Set to a Gmail message ID to forward that message instead of composing a new one. The original subject, body, and (optionally) attachments are carried over; 'body' becomes an optional note prepended to the forward.

include_forwarded_attachments.description: When forwarding, whether to include the original message's attachments. Ignored unless forward_message_id is set.

from_name.description: Optional sender display name (e.g., 'Peter Hartree'). If provided, the From header will be formatted as 'Name <email>'.

from_email.description: Optional 'Send As' alias email address. Must be configured in Gmail settings (Settings > Accounts > Send mail as). If not provided, uses the authenticated user's email.

thread_id.description: Optional Gmail thread ID to reply within. When in_reply_to is omitted, replies to the latest non-draft, non-trash message with an RFC Message-ID.

in_reply_to.description: Optional RFC Message-ID to explicitly reply to a specific message (e.g., '<message123@gmail.com>'). Omit to reply to the latest eligible message in thread_id.

references.description: Optional Message-ID ancestry chain. Normally omit when thread_id is provided; the server derives the chain through the selected reply target.

attachments.description: Optional list of attachments. Each can have: "url" (fetch from URL — works with MCP attachment URLs from get_drive_file_download_url / get_gmail_attachment_content), OR "path" (file path, auto-encodes), OR "content" (standard base64, not urlsafe) + "filename". Optional "mime_type". Optional "content_id" (string) makes the attachment inline-rendered: it lands in a multipart/related part with `Content-ID: ` and `Content-Disposition: inline`, and the HTML body can reference it via `` (RFC 2392). Without `content_id` the attachment is a regular multipart/mixed attachment. Example: [{"url": "https://host/attachments/abc-123", "filename": "report.pdf"}]

include_signature.description: Whether to append the Gmail signature from Settings > Signature when available. Defaults to true.

quote_original.description: Whether to include the message being replied to as a quoted original. Only has an effect when thread_id is provided. Defaults to false.

reply_all.description: Whether to derive reply-all recipients from the thread: To = the sender being replied to, Cc = the other participants, excluding the authenticated account and from_email. Requires thread_id. Explicit to/cc win; when cc is omitted the sender being replied to is added to the derived Cc if they are not already in To. Defaults to false.

tools.name: mcp__gmail__start_google_auth
tools.description:
Manually initiate Google OAuth authentication flow.

NOTE: This is a legacy OAuth 2.0 tool and is disabled when OAuth 2.1 is enabled.
The authentication system automatically handles credential checks and prompts for
authentication when needed. Only use this tool if:
1. You need to re-authenticate with different credentials
2. You want to proactively authenticate before using other tools
3. The automatic authentication flow failed and you need to retry

In most cases, simply try calling the Google Workspace tool you need - it will
automatically handle authentication if required.

# Hermes Home

**Alexa+ on the front. Hermes as the agent underneath.**

> Amazon Developer Hackathon — **Alexa+ track** (self-hosted MCP server, Streamable HTTP, spec 2025-11-25) · also entered in the **Open Source** mini challenge (MIT).

Alexa+ integrates through remote **Streamable-HTTP MCP servers**; the Hermes personal-agent
runtime only ships a stdio MCP server. Hermes Home is the bridge: it exposes a small,
hand-picked set of tools to Alexa+ and keeps every long task asynchronous, so a voice
assistant never waits on a slow agent.

![Alexa+ simulator calling Hermes Home over MCP](docs/img/simulator.jpg)

## Try it in 2 minutes (simulated Alexa+)

No Alexa+ Preview access is needed. `apps/dashboard` contains an **Alexa+ simulator**: a voice/chat
web app that acts as the MCP *client* (official `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`), lists the server's tools,
calls them over Streamable HTTP, and shows every `tools/call` in a live trace panel.

```powershell
npm install
copy .env.example .env      # set HERMES_API_URL / HERMES_API_KEY (and PORT if 3000 is busy)
npm run demo                # tunnel -> MCP bridge -> simulator, verified
# open http://127.0.0.1:3100/sim
```

Things to say: *"Ask Hermes what a good question to reflect on today is"* ·
*"Send me a message on Discord with a question to think about"* ·
*"Ask Hermes to plan a productive Saturday"* → *"Is Hermes done?"*

Optional: set `GOOGLE_API_KEY` and the simulator lets Gemini pick tools by function-calling (like real Alexa+);
without it a keyword router is used. Anything that mentions "Hermes" is routed straight to the agent.

## What is exposed (14 tools — never the whole Hermes catalogue)

`hermes_ask` · `hermes_start_task` · `hermes_task_status` · `hermes_task_result` · `home_get_state` ·
`home_control` (two-step confirm) · `hermes_memory_search` · `hermes_remember` · `calendar_today` ·
`calendar_tomorrow` · `calendar_events` · `github_my_issues` · `github_repo_issues` · `send_message`.
Calendar, Home Assistant and GitHub activate when their credentials are in `.env`; otherwise they
return a clear "not configured" result.

# 🐝 Bee Nav

**Say "find me…" to your Bee — get back an answer and directions.**

Bee Nav hears the navigation-style stuff you say out loud to your Bee wearable ("find me a quiet cafe I haven't been to", "take me to a park across town") and turns it into a chosen destination plus a Google Maps route. It uses your *real* Bee data — current location and where you've actually been — so the suggestion is personal, not generic.

```
  🐝 you: "find me a quiet cafe I haven't been to"
        │  Bee CLI / MCP
        ▼
  Bee Nav bridge
        ├── Strands Agents SDK on Amazon Bedrock  (reasoning & tool use)
        ├── get_current_bee_location()            (Bee context)
        ├── get_recent_bee_visits()               (Bee context)
        ├── search_places() ──► Google Places (New)
        └── build_navigation_url() ──► Google Maps
        ▼
  "Lamplight Books & Brew — quiet, 1.4 km away.
   Directions are ready."  →  opens walking route
```

**Privacy, plainly:** your Bee location, visit history, and the utterance are sent to Amazon Bedrock and to Google Places to produce the answer. That's the point of the product — this is not an offline local model, and we don't pretend it is. Nothing is sent anywhere else; the server binds to `127.0.0.1`.

---

## Why "nav"?

Priorities for the Bee track are personal productivity, education, and developer experience. Bee Nav is *personal productivity with the place dimension*: people already use Bee as a memory layer, and the most actionable memory-adjacent question is **"where should I go next?"**. Bee Nav answers it in one shot and hands you the route — no opening three apps, no scrolling a list.

## How the Bee data is actually used (track requirement)

| Bee data | How Bee Nav uses it |
|---|---|
| `bee locations current` | Origin for the Places search + route |
| `bee locations recent` (30-day lookback) |  | **De-duplication**: "haven't been" actually enforces it — won't send you where you went Tuesday |
| `bee now` (recent conversations + utterances) | The bridge polls it for phrases like *"find me / take me / where can I"* and triggers a run |

In code: `src/services/bee.js` shells out to the official Bee CLI (`npm i -g @beeai/cli`, then `bee login`): `bee locations current --json`, `bee locations recent --from <date> --json` and `bee now --json`. A fixture mode (`BEE_SAMPLE=true`) lets anyone run the demo without hardware; the UI labels it loudly.

## Simulated Bee (no device needed)

# What Did I Miss?

A Fire TV AI contextual viewing assistant.

## Credits

Demo film: **Sintel** (c) Blender Foundation | durian.blender.org, licensed [CC BY 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/).
This project is **not endorsed by or affiliated with Blender**. The story index for Sintel (scenes, events, clues) was produced by the project team from the film and is provided for demonstration.

## Problem

People lose track of movies and shows. They check their phone, get interrupted, or simply forget what happened. When they return, they are lost.

## Solution

**What Did I Miss?** is a Fire TV experience that reconstructs the context the viewer missed. It understands:

- exactly what content is playing
- exactly where the viewer is in the timeline
- what was said during the relevant section
- what happened in the current scene
- which earlier story information is relevant
- what characters, objects, clues, and events matter

It never reveals future events. The system behaves like a story-aware memory for television.

## Features

- **Timestamp-aware recap** — knows exactly where you are
- **Spoiler-safe story memory** — never leaks future events
- **Subtitle-aware retrieval** — uses dialogue as data
- **Scene understanding** — connects what happened to where it happened
- **Character/context memory** — tracks who knows what, when
- **Visual context** — uses keyframes for richer understanding
- **Exact missed-range replay** — jump back to the exact moment you missed

**Privacy, plainly:** your Bee location, visit history, and the utterance are sent to Amazon Bedrock and to Google Places to produce the answer. That's the point of the product — this is not an offline local model, and we don't pretend it is. Nothing is sent anywhere else; the server binds to `127.0.0.1`.

---

## Why "nav"?

Priorities for the Bee track are personal productivity, education, and developer experience. Bee Nav is *personal productivity with the place dimension*: people already use Bee as a memory layer, and the most actionable memory-adjacent question is **"where should I go next?"**. Bee Nav answers it in one shot and hands you the route — no opening three apps, no scrolling a list.

## How the Bee data is actually used (track requirement)

| Bee data | How Bee Nav uses it |
|---|---|
| `bee locations current` | Origin for the Places search + route |
| `bee locations recent` (30-day lookback) |  | **De-duplication**: "haven't been" actually enforces it — won't send you where you went Tuesday |
| `bee now` (recent conversations + utterances) | The bridge polls it for phrases like *"find me / take me / where can I"* and triggers a run |

In code: `src/services/bee.js` shells out to the official Bee CLI (`npm i -g @beeai/cli`, then `bee login`): `bee locations current --json`, `bee locations recent --from <date> --json` and `bee now --json`. A fixture mode (`BEE_SAMPLE=true`) lets anyone run the demo without hardware; the UI labels it loudly.

## Problem

People lose track of movies and shows. They check their phone, get interrupted, or simply forget what happened. When they return, they are lost.

## Solution

**What Did I Miss?** is a Fire TV experience that reconstructs the context the viewer missed. It understands:

- exactly what content is playing
- exactly where the viewer is in the timeline
- what was said during the relevant section
- what happened in the current scene
- which earlier story information is relevant
- what characters, objects, clues, and events matter

It never reveals future events. The system behaves like a story-aware memory for television.

- **Timestamp-aware recap** — knows exactly where you are
- **Spoiler-safe story memory** — never leaks future events
- **Subtitle-aware retrieval** — uses dialogue as data
- **Scene understanding** — connects what happened to where it happened
- **Character/context memory** — tracks who knows what, when
- **Visual context** — uses keyframes for richer understanding
- **Exact missed-range replay** — jump back to the exact moment you missed

I found the judging criteria for the Nebius x NVIDIA Global AI Hackathon. Here's a summary of the rules and requirements.

**Judging criteria**
- A recap of the Amsterdam event, which takes its rules from the official Devpost page, lists four equally weighted criteria: Technological Implementation, Design, Potential Impact and Quality of the Idea. The search results cut off the "Judging Criteria" section of the Devpost listing, so I couldn't check the full description of each criterion. It's on nebiusglobalaihackathon.devpost.com.
- A third-party listing suggests you pick one of the four categories early and build for its criteria rather than trying to be impressive in general.

**Core requirement (Token Factory + Nemotron)**
- Entrants must create a working software application that runs on either Nebius Token Factory or Nebius AI Cloud and uses at least one NVIDIA open source model, and that fits into one of the four hackathon tracks.
- "Runs on Nebius Token Factory or Nebius AI Cloud" means the project makes a runtime call to the Token Factory inference API, or is deployed/run using Nebius AI Cloud compute (Serverless Jobs, Serverless Endpoints, or DevPods).
- The accepted NVIDIA open source models are Nemotron, GR00T, Cosmos, or Sonic.

**Tracks**
1. **Coding and Agentic Engineering**: "Coding agents and developer tools that write, run, and test code in Token Factory Sandboxes."
2. Best Apps and Agents Track: Build any app or agent someone would actually use, from a productivity tool or copilot to a workflow that runs itself. Power it with Nemotron models on Nebius through Token Factory.
3. **Personal AI**: "A private, always-on assistant with memory, reusable skills, and user-controlled tools."
4. Physical AI.

**What to submit**
- A URL to a working demo, hosted application, or test build of your Project (not required for Physical AI submissions).
- A publicly accessible code repository URL (GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket) for judging and testing. The repository must include an open source license (such as Apache 2.0, MIT, or MPL 2.0), visible at the top of the repository page.
- Make sure to highlight how you've used NVIDIA Nemotron or other NVIDIA open source models and where Token Factory accelerated your workflow and any other Nebius Tools or Services used.
- A demo video that should be less than three (3) minutes. Judges are not required to watch beyond three minutes.
- Feedback on Nebius Token Factory, AI Cloud, and any NVIDIA tools, models, or technologies used.

**Key dates**
- Submission period: 26 August 2026, 9:00 am PT, to 30 October 2026, 10:00 am PT. That's about 20 days from today.
- Judging: 2026-12-01 09:00 PT through 2026-12-15 12:00 PT. Your demo needs to stay working and accessible for that whole period.

**Credits**
- You can get $25 in credits by filling out the Nebius promo form with activation code NEBIUS-DEVPOST-GLOBAL26. A second $25 in Token Factory credit (plus Tavily and other credit) comes from joining the free Nebius Builders Program.
- For reference, a community starter repo's default Token Factory model is nvidia/nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b.

# Nebius x NVIDIA Global AI Hackathon: ideas and plan to win

- **Deadline:** Oct 30, 2026, 10:30 pm IST (10:00 am PT). As of Oct 10 that leaves 20 days.
- **Judging:** Dec 1–15, 2026. The hosted demo must stay up the whole time.
- **Rules page:** https://nebiusglobalaihackathon.devpost.com/rules (text copy in `official-rules.txt`)
- **Credits:** $25 with promo code `NEBIUS-DEVPOST-GLOBAL26`, and another $25 of Token Factory credit plus Tavily credit from the free Nebius Builders Program.

## How projects are scored

1. **Stage 1 (pass/fail):** the project has to be a real attempt at its track, not "a superficial rebrand of an unrelated idea", and it has to make a runtime call to Token Factory, or run on Nebius AI Cloud, with an NVIDIA open model (Nemotron, GR00T, Cosmos or Sonic).
2. **Stage 2 (four criteria, equal weight):**
   - **Technological Implementation:** how well it's built and how well it uses Token Factory and Nemotron. *This criterion also breaks ties.*
   - **Design:** a complete product, not just a proof of concept.
   - **Potential Impact:** a specific, believable case for a real audience, backed by what the demo shows.
   - **Quality of the Idea:** a creative, non-obvious use of the models, and real understanding of the problem.
3. **Prize stacking:** a project wins **one Overall award, OR one Track award plus one Bonus award.** Tavily ($3,000) is a Bonus award, so it stacks with a track win.
4. **Easy money:** 10 × $100 go to the most useful feedback. Write a detailed feedback section.
5. **City award:** you only qualify if you attended an IRL event. None was in India, so skip it.

About 20,000 people have signed up. A public starter ("Hermes Buddy": Vite/React + Hono + Nemotron + Tavily) means a flood of near-identical chat assistants, especially in Personal AI. **Don't build a chatbot.**

---

## Idea 1 (recommended): Greenlight, an agent that does breaking dependency upgrades

**Track:** Coding & Agentic Engineering, plus the **Tavily bonus**

**The problem.** Dependabot and Renovate open version-bump PRs, and the major-version ones break the build. Teams ignore them, and security debt piles up. Every engineer judging this has felt that.

**What it does**
1. Takes a repo and an outdated dependency, for example `pydantic 1 → 2` or `express 4 → 5`.
2. Uses **Tavily** to fetch the changelog, migration guide and GitHub release notes for exactly that version range.
3. **Nemotron 3 Ultra** reads them and writes a migration plan: which APIs changed and which files are affected.
4. **Nemotron Super** makes the code edits.
5. The agent runs install, build and tests in a sandbox (Token Factory sandboxes if they're available, otherwise a Nebius Serverless Job).
6. **Nemotron Nano** shrinks failing logs down to the actual error, and the loop repeats until the tests pass.
7. It opens a PR that says what changed and why, with a link to the source for each change.

**What wins the demo.** A real repo goes from red to green in about 2 minutes, on screen. Next to it, a scoreboard: "Ran 25 real upgrades: 19 green, average $0.04 per upgrade, 71% of tokens on Nano." That routing and cost panel is exactly what the track description asks for ("Ultra for serious reasoning, Nano/Super for everyday calls").

**Why it scores on every criterion**
- *Tech:* the agent runs code, checks it and loops, routes across three model tiers, and makes runtime Tavily calls.
- *Design:* a GitHub App plus a web dashboard. Judges paste a public repo URL and watch it work.
- *Impact:* every software team has this problem, and the eval numbers measure it.
- *Idea:* it reads migration guides from the web. That's a non-obvious reason to need search.

**Risks.** Sandbox time and credit cost. Mitigation: start with **one ecosystem** (Python, or JS/TS) and a curated list of 20–30 real upgrade cases.

---

## Idea 2: Appeal, an agent that fights denied insurance claims

**Track:** Best Apps & Agents, plus the **Tavily bonus**

**The problem.** Insurers deny claims, almost nobody appeals, and a large share of the appeals that do get filed succeed. Pull the current KFF and IRDAI figures before you quote any numbers. The audience is concrete and the stakes are emotional.

**What it does**
1. Takes the denial letter, the EOB and the policy PDF. A Nemotron vision model (Nano VL) pulls out the denial code, the reason and the appeal deadline.
2. **Tavily** finds the insurer's clinical policy, the relevant regulations and the medical guidelines.
3. **Ultra** writes an appeal letter that cites those sources.
4. **Super** produces a checklist of what to get from the doctor.
5. **Nano** tracks the deadline and drafts follow-ups.
6. Optional: run follow-ups as a Nebius Serverless Job.

**What wins the demo.** A real-looking (synthetic) denial goes in, and 60 seconds later out comes a cited appeal letter and a countdown to the deadline.

**Risks.** Medical and legal liability, so present it as a drafting assistant. Use synthetic documents only, never real patient data. It could support the US and India (IRDAI / Insurance Ombudsman) to show reach.

---

## Idea 3: Paper Trail, a private life-admin assistant

**Track:** Personal AI. You have an edge here from Hermes Home, but the track is crowded.

**What it does.** You forward it any bill, warranty, lease, policy or subscription. It remembers all of it (persistent memory) and runs inside **NemoClaw/OpenShell** so the data stays under your control.

It warns you before deadlines: "your warranty expires in 9 days", "the trial converts tomorrow". It also answers questions like "is my laptop still covered?" and drafts the cancel, claim or return email.

Its skills are reusable: cancel-subscription, file-warranty-claim, dispute-charge.

**Why only #3.** The Hermes Buddy starter will flood this track. To stand out you'd need real always-on behaviour (Serverless Jobs on a schedule) and a strong privacy story.

---

## Wildcard: Physical AI

This track gets the fewest entries, so it's the best odds for the Jetson track prize, but the hardest route to the grand prize. If you have no hardware, the rules accept footage of "the key application modules in action". For example, use Cosmos to generate synthetic edge-case footage that evaluates a Nemotron-driven inspection agent, with the batches run as Serverless Jobs. GPU cost against $50 of credit is the risk.

---

## Checklist for whichever idea you pick

- [ ] Route across **Ultra, Super and Nano** on purpose, and **show it in the UI** (tokens, cost and latency per tier).
- [ ] Make at least one runtime **Tavily** call that the product actually depends on.
- [ ] Deploy on **Nebius Serverless Endpoints** and do background work with **Serverless Jobs**. This is extra Nebius usage judges can see.
- [ ] Build an **eval harness** and put the real numbers in the README. "Is the impact credible?" gets answered with data.
- [ ] Hosted demo that **stays up until Dec 15**. Leave credit for it, add rate limits, and include a cached sample run.
- [ ] Public repo with an **MIT/Apache license** visible at the top, and a README with setup steps plus sections titled "How we used Nemotron" and "Where Token Factory helped".
- [ ] **Video under 3 minutes.** Show the result in the first 20 seconds, then how it works, then the numbers.
- [ ] A detailed **feedback section** (10 × $100).
- [ ] Get both $25 credit grants on day 1.

## Rough 20-day plan

| Days | Goal |
|---|---|
| 1–2 | Get credits, list the Token Factory models, check that sandboxes exist, build a skeleton that makes one end-to-end call |
| 3–9 | Core agent loop and model routing, plus Tavily |
| 10–13 | Eval harness, run it on the real cases, fix what fails |
| 14–16 | UI polish, hosted deploy, cost panel |
| 17–18 | README, architecture diagram, feedback write-up |
| 19 | Record the video |
| 20 | Submit, with a 1-day buffer before the deadline |

- **Judging:** Dec 1–15, 2026. The hosted demo must stay up the whole time.
- **Rules page:** https://nebiusglobalaihackathon.devpost.com/rules (text copy in `official-rules.txt`)
- **Credits:** $25 with promo code `NEBIUS-DEVPOST-GLOBAL26`, and another $25 of Token Factory credit plus Tavily credit from the free Nebius Builders Program.

## How projects are scored

1. **Stage 1 (pass/fail):** the project has to be a real attempt at its track, not "a superficial rebrand of an unrelated idea", and it has to make a runtime call to Token Factory, or run on Nebius AI Cloud, with an NVIDIA open model (Nemotron, GR00T, Cosmos or Sonic).
2. **Stage 2 (four criteria, equal weight):**
   - **Technological Implementation:** how well it's built and how well it uses Token Factory and Nemotron. *This criterion also breaks ties.*
   - **Design:** a complete product, not just a proof of concept.
   - **Potential Impact:** a specific, believable case for a real audience, backed by what the demo shows.
   - **Quality of the Idea:** a creative, non-obvious use of the models, and real understanding of the problem.
3. **Prize stacking:** a project wins **one Overall award, OR one Track award plus one Bonus award.** Tavily ($3,000) is a Bonus award, so it stacks with a track win.
4. **Easy money:** 10 × $100 go to the most useful feedback. Write a detailed feedback section.
5. **City award:** you only qualify if you attended an IRL event. None was in India, so skip it.

About 20,000 people have signed up. A public starter ("Hermes Buddy": Vite/React + Hono + Nemotron + Tavily) means a flood of near-identical chat assistants, especially in Personal AI. **Don't build a chatbot.**

---

## Idea 1 (recommended): Greenlight, an agent that does breaking dependency upgrades

**Track:** Coding & Agentic Engineering, plus the **Tavily bonus**

**The problem.** Dependabot and Renovate open version-bump PRs, and the major-version ones break the build. Teams ignore them, and security debt piles up. Every engineer judging this has felt that.

**What it does**
1. Takes a repo and an outdated dependency, for example `pydantic 1 → 2` or `express 4 → 5`.
2. Uses **Tavily** to fetch the changelog, migration guide and GitHub release notes for exactly that version range.
3. **Nemotron 3 Ultra** reads them and writes a migration plan: which APIs changed and which files are affected.
4. **Nemotron Super** makes the code edits.
5. The agent runs install, build and tests in a sandbox (Token Factory sandboxes if they're available, otherwise a Nebius Serverless Job).
6. **Nemotron Nano** shrinks failing logs down to the actual error, and the loop repeats until the tests pass.
7. It opens a PR that says what changed and why, with a link to the source for each change.

**What wins the demo.** A real repo goes from red to green in about 2 minutes, on screen. Next to it, a scoreboard: "Ran 25 real upgrades: 19 green, average $0.04 per upgrade, 71% of tokens on Nano." That routing and cost panel is exactly what the track description asks for ("Ultra for serious reasoning, Nano/Super for everyday calls").

**Why it scores on every criterion**
- *Tech:* the agent runs code, checks it and loops, routes across three model tiers, and makes runtime Tavily calls.
- *Design:* a GitHub App plus a web dashboard. Judges paste a public repo URL and watch it work.
- *Impact:* every software team has this problem, and the eval numbers measure it.
- *Idea:* it reads migration guides from the web. That's a non-obvious reason to need search.

**Risks.** Sandbox time and credit cost. Mitigation: start with **one ecosystem** (Python, or JS/TS) and a curated list of 20–30 real upgrade cases.

---

## Idea 2: Appeal, an agent that fights denied insurance claims

**Track:** Best Apps & Agents, plus the **Tavily bonus**

**The problem.** Insurers deny claims, almost nobody appeals, and a large share of the appeals that do get filed succeed. Pull the current KFF and IRDAI figures before you quote any numbers. The audience is concrete and the stakes are emotional.

**What it does**
1. Takes the denial letter, the EOB and the policy PDF. A Nemotron vision model (Nano VL) pulls out the denial code, the reason and the appeal deadline.
2. **Tavily** finds the insurer's clinical policy, the relevant regulations and the medical guidelines.
3. **Ultra** writes an appeal letter that cites those sources.
4. **Super** produces a checklist of what to get from the doctor.
5. **Nano** tracks the deadline and drafts follow-ups.
6. Optional: run follow-ups as a Nebius Serverless Job.

**What wins the demo.** A real-looking (synthetic) denial goes in, and 60 seconds later out comes a cited appeal letter and a countdown to the deadline.

**Risks.** Medical and legal liability, so present it as a drafting assistant. Use synthetic documents only, never real patient data. It could support the US and India (IRDAI / Insurance Ombudsman) to show reach.

---

## Idea 3: Paper Trail, a private life-admin assistant

**Track:** Personal AI. You have an edge here from Hermes Home, but the track is crowded.

**What it does.** You forward it any bill, warranty, lease, policy or subscription. It remembers all of it (persistent memory) and runs inside **NemoClaw/OpenShell** so the data stays under your control.

It warns you before deadlines: "your warranty expires in 9 days", "the trial converts tomorrow". It also answers questions like "is my laptop still covered?" and drafts the cancel, claim or return email.

Its skills are reusable: cancel-subscription, file-warranty-claim, dispute-charge.

**Why only #3.** The Hermes Buddy starter will flood this track. To stand out you'd need real always-on behaviour (Serverless Jobs on a schedule) and a strong privacy story.

---

## Wildcard: Physical AI

This track gets the fewest entries, so it's the best odds for the Jetson track prize, but the hardest route to the grand prize. If you have no hardware, the rules accept footage of "the key application modules in action". For example, use Cosmos to generate synthetic edge-case footage that evaluates a Nemotron-driven inspection agent, with the batches run as Serverless Jobs. GPU cost against $50 of credit is the risk.

---

## Checklist for whichever idea you pick

- [ ] Route across **Ultra, Super and Nano** on purpose, and **show it in the UI** (tokens, cost and latency per tier).
- [ ] Make at least one runtime **Tavily** call that the product actually depends on.
- [ ] Deploy on **Nebius Serverless Endpoints** and do background work with **Serverless Jobs**. This is extra Nebius usage judges can see.
- [ ] Build an **eval harness** and put the real numbers in the README. "Is the impact credible?" gets answered with data.
- [ ] Hosted demo that **stays up until Dec 15**. Leave credit for it, add rate limits, and include a cached sample run.
- [ ] Public repo with an **MIT/Apache license** visible at the top, and a README with setup steps plus sections titled "How we used Nemotron" and "Where Token Factory helped".
- [ ] **Video under 3 minutes.** Show the result in the first 20 seconds, then how it works, then the numbers.
- [ ] A detailed **feedback section** (10 × $100).
- [ ] Get both $25 credit grants on day 1.

## Rough 20-day plan

| Days | Goal |
|---|---|
| 1–2 | Get credits, list the Token Factory models, check that sandboxes exist, build a skeleton that makes one end-to-end call |
| 3–9 | Core agent loop and model routing, plus Tavily |
| 10–13 | Eval harness, run it on the real cases, fix what fails |
| 14–16 | UI polish, hosted deploy, cost panel |
| 17–18 | README, architecture diagram, feedback write-up |
| 19 | Record the video |
| 20 | Submit, with a 1-day buffer before the deadline |

No API keys available, and Docker's installed but the daemon isn't running. Since the user favors TypeScript/Node monorepos, I'm sketching out a structure while research runs: a `packages/core` for the agent, a web dashboard app, a CLI app, and an evals package, with Node 24 as the runtime. I'm also weighing which ecosystem to target first, possibly Python.

Weighing JS vs Python for the demo migrations: Python's pydantic v1→v2 is a famous, well-documented painful upgrade with official tooling, and numpy 2.0, pandas 2.0, SQLAlchemy 1.4→2.0, Flask, and marshmallow all offer strong breaking-change eval cases, especially with uv making installs fast and deterministic. JS alternatives like express 4→5 or react-router 5→6 exist too, but I'm leaning toward Python first for its richer set of iconic migrations, with JS as a secondary ecosystem if time allows. I'm also considering whether the agent itself should be written in Python versus TypeScript, since the sandbox can run either language's tooling regardless.

For the actual build, I'm deciding on a TypeScript monorepo: a Hono server with a Vite React dashboard, and the agent core also in TS to keep things to one language. I still need to confirm sandbox availability -- falling back to local Docker, Nebius Serverless Jobs (preferred for credits), or e2b if needed. For the evaluation set, I want real open-source repos pinned at commits using older package versions with existing tests, where success means tests pass after upgrade without the agent gaming it by deleting or modifying test files -- so I need a guardrail disallowing test file changes in the diff.

The agent loop itself: clone the repo at the pinned commit, detect the package manager and test command, establish a baseline pass set, bump the dependency and confirm the tests go red, then research the migration using Tavily to pull guides and release notes for the version range, caching that content for reuse.

From there, Super distills the guide into a rule sheet scoped to the APIs actually used in the repo (grepping usages first), Ultra turns that rule sheet plus usage sites and a compressed failure log into an edit plan, and Super executes edits via tool calls with read/search/apply-edit/run-tests, looping back through Ultra/Super with Nano-compressed error logs on failure up to a max iteration count. Finally it verifies the guardrails, produces a diff and PR body citing the guide sections for each change, and optionally opens a PR via the GitHub API.

Thinking through model routing now: Nano handles log triage, page summarization, and usage classification; Super handles the code-edit tool loop; Ultra handles planning and gets escalated to after two failed iterations, with per-call tokens/cost/latency recorded for a telemetry panel. I'm also sketching the web UI — picking a demo case or pasting a repo, live SSE streaming of research, plan, diffs, test runs, and model routing stats, plus a scoreboard page — hosted on a Nebius serverless endpoint with sandboxed runs, rate limiting, and cached replay for judges.

For live demo access, I'm considering gating it behind a passcode, limiting live runs to curated cases plus rate limits, while always allowing replay. On the GitHub integration side, I'm leaning toward a bot token that forks and opens PRs against our own forks of the eval repos, giving visible proof like "19 real PRs opened." I'm also planning a CLI that mirrors the web flow locally, sharing the same core, with a possible GitHub Action down the line — all fitting into a 20-day solo timeline, and I want to wait for the research results before locking anything in.

While that's pending, I should kick off a parallel task to find around 25 real public Python repos pinned to older versions of pydantic, numpy, pandas, or sqlalchemy that have fast pytest suites without external service dependencies — I'm committed enough to Python as the target ecosystem to launch this candidate-search agent now regardless of sandbox image details.

input.prompt:
Research task: build the evaluation set for a hackathon project. Accuracy matters: these cases will be run for real, so every claim must come from actually inspecting the repo (use `gh` CLI, which is logged in, and/or `git clone --depth` into a scratch dir under %TEMP%; don't run their code).

Project: "Greenlight", an AI agent that performs breaking major-version dependency upgrades on Python repos (bump the dep, read the migration guide, edit code, run pytest until green). We need ~30 candidate real public GitHub repos (small/medium) that are STILL on an old major version of one of these libraries, where upgrading will break code:
- pydantic v1 → v2 (pinned `pydantic<2` or `pydantic==1.*`, uses `@validator`, `.dict()`, `class Config`, `parse_obj`, etc.)
- numpy 1 → 2 (uses removed aliases like `np.float_`, `np.NaN`, `np.Inf`, `np.product`, `np.in1d` etc., pinned `numpy<2`)
- pandas 1 → 2 (uses `DataFrame.append`, `iteritems`, `swaplevel` defaults, etc., pinned `pandas<2`)
- SQLAlchemy 1.x → 2.0 (legacy `query` patterns, `engine.execute`, pinned `sqlalchemy<2`)
- Also acceptable: marshmallow 3→4, Flask 2→3 / Werkzeug, httpx, or other well-known breaking majors with an official migration guide.

Requirements for each good candidate:
- Has a pytest (or unittest) suite that should run offline in < ~3 min with no external services (no Postgres/Redis/network; sqlite OK).
- Dependencies installable with pip/uv on Linux, Python 3.10–3.12 (no heavy C builds, no GPU, no CUDA).
- Repo is small/medium (< ~20k LOC), MIT/Apache/BSD license preferred.
- Actually uses the breaking APIs (grep for them and cite file paths + counts).

Use GitHub code search via `gh search code` (e.g. `gh search code "pydantic<2" --filename requirements.txt`, `gh search code "np.float_" --language python`) and `gh search repos`. Prefer repos with real tests and recent-ish activity (2022+).

Output: a markdown table with columns: repo URL, pinned commit SHA (HEAD at time of inspection), library + from→to, manifest file, evidence (breaking APIs found with counts), test command, est. test runtime/risk notes, license. Rank by suitability. Then list rejected repos briefly with the reason. Aim for 30 candidates (at least 8 per library for pydantic, numpy and pandas). Save the full result to `D:\hackathn fire tv\nebius nvidia global ai\research\eval-candidates.md` (create the folder), and return a short summary plus the top 10.

toolUseResult.prompt:
Research task: build the evaluation set for a hackathon project. Accuracy matters: these cases will be run for real, so every claim must come from actually inspecting the repo (use `gh` CLI, which is logged in, and/or `git clone --depth` into a scratch dir under %TEMP%; don't run their code).

Project: "Greenlight", an AI agent that performs breaking major-version dependency upgrades on Python repos (bump the dep, read the migration guide, edit code, run pytest until green). We need ~30 candidate real public GitHub repos (small/medium) that are STILL on an old major version of one of these libraries, where upgrading will break code:
- pydantic v1 → v2 (pinned `pydantic<2` or `pydantic==1.*`, uses `@validator`, `.dict()`, `class Config`, `parse_obj`, etc.)
- numpy 1 → 2 (uses removed aliases like `np.float_`, `np.NaN`, `np.Inf`, `np.product`, `np.in1d` etc., pinned `numpy<2`)
- pandas 1 → 2 (uses `DataFrame.append`, `iteritems`, `swaplevel` defaults, etc., pinned `pandas<2`)
- SQLAlchemy 1.x → 2.0 (legacy `query` patterns, `engine.execute`, pinned `sqlalchemy<2`)
- Also acceptable: marshmallow 3→4, Flask 2→3 / Werkzeug, httpx, or other well-known breaking majors with an official migration guide.

Requirements for each good candidate:
- Has a pytest (or unittest) suite that should run offline in < ~3 min with no external services (no Postgres/Redis/network; sqlite OK).
- Dependencies installable with pip/uv on Linux, Python 3.10–3.12 (no heavy C builds, no GPU, no CUDA).
- Repo is small/medium (< ~20k LOC), MIT/Apache/BSD license preferred.
- Actually uses the breaking APIs (grep for them and cite file paths + counts).

Use GitHub code search via `gh search code` (e.g. `gh search code "pydantic<2" --filename requirements.txt`, `gh search code "np.float_" --language python`) and `gh search repos`. Prefer repos with real tests and recent-ish activity (2022+).

Output: a markdown table with columns: repo URL, pinned commit SHA (HEAD at time of inspection), library + from→to, manifest file, evidence (breaking APIs found with counts), test command, est. test runtime/risk notes, license. Rank by suitability. Then list rejected repos briefly with the reason. Aim for 30 candidates (at least 8 per library for pydantic, numpy and pandas). Save the full result to `D:\hackathn fire tv\nebius nvidia global ai\research\eval-candidates.md` (create the folder), and return a short summary plus the top 10.

Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\cocat\.claude\skills\brave-browser-control

# Brave browser control

Browser control here means Manu's **own Brave window, profile "Default" (Personal)**, driven through the
**Playwright Extension** (id `mmlmfjhmonkocbjadbfplnigmagldckm`). His logins are there, and he can
watch by opening the agent window, but by default it all runs in the background (see below). Anything else (headless, `--isolated`, T3 preview, `mcp__t3-code__preview_*`) is signed out and
invisible to him, so it is wrong for this job.

## The only correct server config

User-scope MCP server `brave` in `~/.claude.json`:

```
command: node
args: C:\Users\cocat\.local\playwright-mcp\mcp-supervisor.cjs     (supervisor, see below)
      C:\Users\cocat\.local\playwright-mcp\node_modules\@playwright\mcp\cli.js
      --extension
      --executable-path C:/Program Files/BraveSoftware/Brave-Browser/Application/brave.exe
      --profile-dir-name Default
      --caps vision,pdf,devtools,storage
      --output-dir C:\Users\cocat\.local\playwright-mcp\output
env:  PLAYWRIGHT_MCP_EXTENSION_TOKEN=<token from the extension>
```

`mcp-supervisor.cjs` (added 2026-10-10) runs cli.js as a child and restarts it transparently when it
dies or when `coreBundle.js` is patched (once idle), replaying the MCP handshake, so open chats never
need `/mcp`. A call running when the child dies gets "The browser server restarted… retry if
needed". Log: `playwright-mcp/supervisor.log`. Test: `node patches/test-supervisor.cjs`. Re-add with
`node patches/use-supervisor.cjs` if the entry is ever rewritten. Chats started before the switch
still run the old command until their next `/mcp` or restart.

**Never** change it to `--headless` or `--isolated`, never drop `--extension` or the token, and never
"fix" a browser problem by switching modes. On 2026-10-09 some session did exactly that, every thread
silently drove an invisible signed-out browser, and Manu couldn't see anything. If you need a throwaway
headless browser for QA, use puppeteer-core in a script, not this server.

## Background mode (never steal Manu's screen)

Manu's rule: browser work must happen silently, never pulling Brave to the front or switching his tab.
Set up on 2026-10-10 (all under `C:\Users\cocat\.local\playwright-mcp\`):

- `extension-bg/`: local build of the extension (same ID/token, loaded unpacked in Brave). It never
  activates tabs, focuses or creates windows (on Windows any new Brave window steals focus). Agent tabs
  are **background tabs** in a collapsed "Playwright" group chip in Manu's window, closed when the MCP
  server disconnects. Rebuild after an extension update with `node patches/build-extension.cjs`, then
  `curl -X POST 127.0.0.1:8770/reload`. If Brave shows "Service worker registration failed" or
  `chrome.X` undefined, he must Remove + Load unpacked again (a plain reload keeps stale settings).
- `broker.cjs` (port 8770, autostarts from `Startup\playwright-broker.vbs`): MCP servers ask it to open
  the connect page through the extension instead of launching `brave.exe` (which always raises Brave).
  `curl 127.0.0.1:8770/status` → `{"extension":true}` when wired up; log in `broker.log`.
- `patches/apply.cjs`: playwright-core patches (re-run after any Playwright update, then `/mcp`):
  broker connect (and never launching `brave.exe` while Brave runs), background new tabs, no
  `bringToFront` on tab switch, instant stable-check and DOM-event clicks/wheel in hidden tabs,
  upload fallback + `browser_set_input_files`. Verified 2026-10-10 on saucedemo (login, add to cart,
  sort) + react-dropzone upload with focus logged: no agent tab ever came to the front.

### Safeguards (what happens when things go wrong)

| Situation | What the setup does | What the agent should do |
|---|---|---|
| Any tool call runs long | Capped at 120 s (`PW_MCP_TOOL_CAP_MS`); page read-back capped at 30 s | Read the error, `browser_snapshot`, continue; never repeat the same call |
| Page stuck in an endless script / hung renderer | After any slow (>4 s) or failed call the tab is pinged; if it doesn't answer in 3 s its JS is terminated, a fresh tab opened and the dead tab closed (also prevents Brave's "Page unresponsive" prompt) | Navigate back and continue |
| Brave freezes the background tab | Hidden agent tabs are kept unfrozen every 2 s | Nothing |
| alert / confirm / prompt | Call returns at once with "Modal state"; self-heal skips tabs with an open dialog | `browser_handle_dialog` |
| Site opens a popup (`target=_blank`, `window.open`, popup window) | Links: default cancelled, URL opened as a background tab. `window.open`: extension switches Manu's tab/window back | Use `browser_tabs` to find it |
| Manu closes the agent's tabs | Connection stays open; next call opens a new tab | Navigate again |
| Extension reloaded / Brave restarted | Next call reconnects through the broker | Retry once |
| Broker dead | Next connect restarts it via `wscript` + `Startup\\playwright-broker.vbs` (detached) | Nothing |
| Extension not connected while Brave runs | Error "background Playwright extension is not connected"; never launches `brave.exe` | Check `curl 127.0.0.1:8770/status`; ask Manu to look at the extension card's Errors |
| Dead host / bad URL | Normal navigation error in <1 s | Report it |

Every stall is appended to `C:\Users\cocat\.local\playwright-mcp\stalls.log`.
**Smoke test** (13 scenarios, real background tabs, checks focus is never taken):
`node C:/Users/cocat/.local/playwright-mcp/patches/smoke.mjs` (add `--skip-disruptive` when other threads
are using the browser: the reload/broker cases briefly drop every agent session). Run it after any
patch, Playwright update or extension rebuild. Last full run 2026-10-10: 13/13 passed except one
non-reproducible focus blip right after the extension-reload case.

**Brave freezes background tabs** (measured: FREEZE 2 s after load, then no timers or network
callbacks, so a site's own JS stalls, e.g. after clicking SEND). `patches/apply.cjs` keeps hidden agent
tabs unfrozen (`Page.setWebLifecycleState active` every 2 s) and caps every tool call at 120 s
(`PW_MCP_TOOL_CAP_MS`). If a call returns "gave up after 120s", take `browser_snapshot` and continue;
don't repeat the call.

**Speed rule: never wait inside the page.** Brave throttles timers in background tabs (≥1 s per
timer, once measured at 7 minutes for a 2 s `setTimeout`). So never put `await new Promise(r =>
setTimeout(r, N))` or polling loops in `browser_evaluate`/`run_code` page functions. Wait with
`browser_wait_for` (`text`, `textGone` or `time`; it waits in Node at full speed) or with Playwright
waits in run_code (`page.waitForSelector`, `locator.waitFor`, `page.waitForURL`), and make evaluate
calls return immediately.

So in agent tabs `document.visibilityState` is normally `"hidden"`; that's expected. In hidden tabs the
patches turn mouse input into DOM events (moves/hover, clicks, double/right clicks, wheel, HTML5
drag-and-drop) and skip the animation-frame/in-page-timer waits Brave throttles there. Verified
2026-10-10 in a real background tab: saucedemo login → cart → checkout (~0.3-1.3 s per tool call),
`browser_drag`, `browser_hover`, `browser_drop` with files, uploads; file pickers opened by clicks are
intercepted (then `browser_file_upload`). Limits: events are untrusted (`isTrusted: false`), CSS
`:hover` styles don't apply, and coordinate clicks don't reach into iframes (use frame locators).
Never call `bringToFront` or start a `brave.exe` yourself. If Manu wants to watch, he can click a tab
in the "Playwright" group. If the server errors with "background Playwright extension is not
connected", check `curl 127.0.0.1:8770/status` and ask Manu to look at the extension card (Errors
button) instead of retrying.

## Hang rule: skip and tell Manu, never keep retrying

A browser tool call that hangs has cost 30 minutes twice (2026-10-09 `mouse.wheel`; 2026-10-10 a
run_code doing `scrollIntoView` + `boundingBox` + `mouse.click` on Do Ventures' SEND, after which the
session dropped and lost its tabs). The `brave` server entry now has `"timeout": 150000` in
`~/.claude.json` (backup `.claude.json.bak-brave-timeout`) so a silent call aborts after 150 s
instead of 30 min; keep it, and don't raise it.

- **Stop signals:** a call that takes more than ~2 min, "gave up after 120s", a tool timeout,
  `Connection closed`, or a connect page / lost tabs after a reconnect. On any of these: do **not**
  retry the same step, loop, or try variants of it. Stop that form/site, mark it
  "skipped (browser hung)" in the tracker/to-do, **tell Manu in the reply**, and move on to the next
  item (or stop if everything else needs the same browser).
- **After a hang you don't know what happened.** Don't resubmit anything. Reopen the page only to
  read state (e.g. a success message), and log the item as "unconfirmed" if you can't see it.
- **Prevent it:** never use `mouse.wheel` (use `window.scrollTo`); keep run_code short (one action
  plus one read, no `scrollIntoView` + coordinate-click chains); click buttons with a plain
  `browser_evaluate` (`el.click()`), which returned instantly where coordinate clicks hung; read
  state with `browser_evaluate`/`browser_snapshot` right after, not inside the same run_code.
- Max one retry of a failed (not hung) step, and only with a different method.

## Check before doing anything

First call in a task: `browser_navigate` to the target, then confirm the session is real:

- the page is signed in (not a login screen) when Manu says he's logged in, and
- `browser_evaluate` → `navigator.userAgent` does **not** contain `HeadlessChrome`.

If either fails, the server is misconfigured. Don't ask Manu to log in again:

1. Inspect: `node -e "console.log(require(process.env.USERPROFILE+'/.claude.json').mcpServers.brave)"`.
2. Restore the `brave` entry from `~/.claude.json.bak-browserfix` (has the good args + token); copy only
   that entry, back up `.claude.json` first.
3. The running thread keeps the old server config in memory. Either reconnect (`/mcp`, new thread), or
   in this thread run `node C:/Users/cocat/.local/playwright-mcp/bridge.mjs` in the background and send
   tool calls with `curl -s 127.0.0.1:8765 -d '{"name":"browser_snapshot","arguments":{}}'`
   (same tool names/args as `mcp__brave__*`; images land in `playwright-mcp/output/bridge-N.png`).

## Rules

- **Not for email.** Reading, sending or checking mail (Gmail included) goes through `python E:\ai\mailhub\mail.py` (the inbox watcher), never this browser. The only exception is Google's permission screen for the watcher script, when Manu asks.

- Never type Manu's passwords or 2FA codes. If a site is signed out, leave the tab on its login page
  and ask him to sign in there.
- Each client sees only its own tab group, not all of his tabs.
- **File uploads work** (pitch decks, images, PDFs; tested 2026-10-09 on Jotform, Typeform, Airtable,
  Uppy, FilePond, Dropzone, react-dropzone, iframes incl. cross-origin, open/closed shadow DOM, unicode
  filenames, 60 MB byte-exact). Brave rejects the native call (`DOM.setFileInputFiles: Not allowed`), so
  `patches/apply.cjs` makes Playwright read the file in Node and inject it. How to upload:
  0. Folders (`<input webkitdirectory>`): pass the folder path as the only entry in `paths` (either
     tool below); every file underneath is uploaded with its `folder/sub/file` relative path.
  1. `browser_set_input_files` with `target` = snapshot ref or a selector like
     `input[type=file] >> nth=0`, plus absolute `paths`. No click; works on hidden inputs. Inputs inside
     an iframe: `iframe#x >> internal:control=enter-frame >> input[type=file]`.
  2. Widgets with no input until opened (Airtable/Uppy dialog "Drop files here or click to browse"):
     `browser_click` the zone (or `locator.dispatchEvent('click')` in run_code), then step 1 on the new
     input (Airtable: `input.uppy-Dashboard-input:not([webkitdirectory]) >> nth=0`, then press its
     "Upload 1 file" button).
  3. `browser_click` the upload button → "[File chooser]" → `browser_file_upload` (works in background
     tabs too). Drop-only zones: `browser_drop` with `paths`.
  Then confirm in the page (filename/preview/"uploaded") before submitting. Caveats: the page sees
  `isTrusted: false` input/change events (no site tested cared); `accept=` isn't enforced, so pick the
  right file type; sites using `window.showOpenFilePicker` (no `<input>`) can't be automated.
- If uploads fail with "Not allowed", `browser_set_input_files` is missing, or Brave starts jumping to
  the front again, Playwright was reinstalled/updated: re-run
  `node C:/Users/cocat/.local/playwright-mcp/patches/apply.cjs` and restart the server (`/mcp`).
- Other extension limits: animated pages can break the "stable" wait in a visible tab (click by
  coordinates from `getBoundingClientRect`).
- Confirm before anything outward-facing (purchases, publishing, sending, deleting).

<result>The main finding is that Token Factory Sandboxes exist, but only as a Beta you must request access to. Everything below was fetched directly, except the items marked UNVERIFIED.

## 1. Token Factory inference API

- **Base URL:** `https://api.tokenfactory.nebius.com/v1/`. The Nebius cookbook and the Nemotron service page use `https://api.tokenfactory.us-central1.nebius.com/v1/`. I confirmed the non-regional host is live (`/v1/models` returned 401 "token is not present" without a key). The regional host was not probed. Use the non-regional one; the docs warn that regional hosts can change.
- **Auth:** `Authorization: Bearer $NEBIUS_API_KEY`.
- **Compatibility:** OpenAI-compatible. The docs use the stock `openai` SDK with `base_url` set. Function calling uses the OpenAI `tools` / `tool_choice` format. `tool_choice` supports `"auto"` or a named function. JSON mode uses `response_format` with `json_schema` or `json_object`, "supported models only" per model card.
- **Which Nemotron models support tools or JSON mode:**
  - Ultra: the cookbook says "Reasoning: Available, Tool calling: Available".
  - Super and Nano 30B: the cookbook says function calling and structured output are supported.
  - Lightning: not stated (UNVERIFIED).
  - Streaming: standard OpenAI API, but I found no Nebius page confirming it (UNVERIFIED).

Source URLs for this section:
- Quickstart: https://docs.tokenfactory.nebius.com/quickstart
- Function calling: https://docs.tokenfactory.nebius.com/ai-models-inference/function-calling
- JSON mode: https://docs.tokenfactory.nebius.com/ai-models-inference/json

**Model IDs.** Sources are the cookbook (https://github.com/nebius/token-factory-cookbook/tree/main/models/nemotron) and the starter repo. IDs are case-sensitive.

| Model | ID | Context | Price per 1M tokens (in/out) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B-A55B | `nvidia/Nemotron-3-Ultra-550b-a55b` | 1M | $1.00 / $3.00 (cookbook) |
| Nemotron 3 Super 120B-A12B | `nvidia/nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b` | 256K hosted (262,144); model supports 1M | $0.30 / $0.90 (secondary source, endpoints page via search; not read directly) |
| Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B | `nvidia/Nemotron-3_5-Lightning` | 1M | UNVERIFIED |
| Nemotron 3 Nano 30B-A3B | `nvidia/nvidia-nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b` in the cookbook; a hackathon repo's live `/v1/models` check shows `nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B` | 262K | UNVERIFIED |
| Nemotron 3 Nano Omni (multimodal) | `nvidia/nemotron-3-nano-omni` | 262K | UNVERIFIED |

- The cookbook comments Nano out as "not currently featured", so it may be gone or hidden. Call `GET /v1/models` with your key before relying on any ID.
- There is no "Nano VL" on the cookbook or Nebius pages I read. Nano Omni is the multimodal model. Treat Nano VL as UNVERIFIED.
- A `-fast` suffix on a model name selects the lower-latency flavor at a different price (https://docs.tokenfactory.nebius.com/ai-models-inference/overview). Whether Nemotron has `-fast` variants is UNVERIFIED.

**Reasoning toggle.**
- Thinking is on by default, with no system-prompt switch.
- The working toggle is `extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}}`. This comes from hackathon repos that tested it live, not from Nebius docs (https://github.com/aiambo08/nebiusxnvidia_hackathon/pull/1). I only read their PR description and could not see the request payloads.
- They report that with thinking on and `max_tokens` around 600, all tokens went to `reasoning_content` and `content` came back empty.
- They also report that a `/no_think` system prompt is ignored. This is second-hand.
- NVIDIA's `low_effort` and `reasoning_budget` options are UNVERIFIED on Nebius.
- If a reply is cut off at `finish_reason == "length"`, reasoning text can leak into `content`. Reject those replies.
- Nebius docs say nothing about this toggle, so test it yourselves.

**Inference call, matching the starter's source:**
```python
from openai import OpenAI
import os
client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.tokenfactory.nebius.com/v1/", api_key=os.environ["NEBIUS_API_KEY"])
r = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="nvidia/nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b",
    messages=[{"role":"user","content":"..."}],
    tools=[...],  # OpenAI format
    extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs":{"enable_thinking": False}},  # per community repos
)
```

**Starter repo** (https://github.com/fruteroclub/nebius-nvidia-ai-hackathon-starter): `server/app.ts` posts to `${NEBIUS_BASE_URL or https://api.tokenfactory.nebius.com}/v1/chat/completions` with default model `nvidia/nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b`. It also calls Tavily at `https://api.tavily.com/search`. It is a Vite + React + Hono template and does not use Sandboxes.

**Rate limits** (https://docs.tokenfactory.nebius.com/ai-models-inference/rate-limits): the example baseline is 60 RPM and 400K TPM. Limits grow 1.2x per 15-minute window when usage stays at or above 80%. A 429 means you are over the limit.

## 2. Token Factory Sandboxes

It exists (https://docs.tokenfactory.nebius.com/sandboxes/overview). It is Nebius's rebranding of "Contree", which the SDK, CLI and MCP package names still use.

- **Status:** **Beta, access must be requested** at https://tokenfactory.nebius.com/sandboxes/about. An API key alone gives a status of "inactive". Feedback and activation go to contree@nebius.com. Request access immediately. The MCP quickstart page calls it "Early Access".
- **Model:** each run is an "operation" that starts a fresh VM-isolated compute from an image, runs one command, and returns stdout, stderr and the exit code. Only filesystem state survives, saved as an immutable image UUID. Processes and memory do not survive. Saving or discarding is chosen up front with `disposable`. You can branch many runs from one image in parallel, which fits the try-patch, test, keep-the-green-branch loop.
- **Packages:** `contree-sdk==0.3.6` (Python, async and sync), `contree-cli==0.9.4` (`contree` command), `contree-mcp`, and REST at `https://api.tokenfactory.nebius.com/sandboxes/v1`. There is no JS SDK, so use REST from Node.
- **Auth:** the same `NEBIUS_API_KEY`, plus the project ID. The SDK and REST read `NEBIUS_PROJECT_ID`. The CLI reads `NEBIUS_AI_PROJECT`. REST sends `Authorization: Bearer` and a `Project: <id>` header.
- **Quickstart (from the docs):**
```python
from contree_sdk import Contree
client = Contree()
base = await client.images.use("alpine:3.19", strict=True)   # or images.oci("docker.io/library/python:3.12-alpine")
r = await base.run(shell="...", cwd="/repo", files={"/repo/calc.py": b"..."},
                   disposable=False, timeout=60)
# r.exit_code, r.stdout, r.stderr, r.uuid (saved image); r.read("/path") -> bytes; r.download(path, local)
nxt = await (await client.images.use(r.uuid, strict=True)).run(shell="pytest", disposable=True, timeout=30)
```
- **REST spawn:** `POST /v1/instances` with `{"image": UUID, "command": "...", "shell": true, "cwd": "/repo", "disposable": true, "timeout": 30, "networking": {"enabled": true}, "env": {...}, "files": {...}}`. It returns 201 with an operation `uuid`. Poll `GET /v1/operations/{id}` until `SUCCESS`, `FAILED` or `CANCELLED`. Then read `metadata.result.state.exit_code` and `result_image_uuid`. A `SUCCESS` operation can still contain a nonzero exit code.
- **Files:** upload with the `files={...}` argument (bytes or local paths). Read results back from the saved image with `image.read()` or `download()`.
- **Git clone and npm:** there is no dedicated git feature. Run `git clone` inside a command.
  - **Network:** the guest network is on by default, and `networking.enabled=false` turns it off. The docs show no allowlists or private networking.
  - **Env:** use `images.oci(...)` to import any Docker Hub image (the cookbook imports `python:3.12-alpine`). Install tools once with `disposable=False` and reuse the saved UUID.
  - **Not tested:** nothing in the docs demonstrates `git clone`, `npm install` or outbound access from inside a sandbox. Treat it as UNVERIFIED until you try it. Also, a node image may lack git, and Alpine images lack it by default.
- **Limits:**
  - 50 simultaneous operations during Beta.
  - Checkpoint images are kept 180 days.
  - Recorded output is 1 MiB per stream by default, up to 10 MiB.
  - The timeout is a per-request field in seconds. The maximum is account-specific, shown by `GET /sandboxes/v1/whoami`.
  - Upload and download size limits are not documented.
- **Pricing:** UNVERIFIED. No public price was found. Operations expose a raw `cost` field, but the docs say not to use it for billing. Ask the Sandboxes team.
- **Hackathon note:** per the Devpost rules, a project qualifies by making a runtime Token Factory inference call or by running on Nebius AI Cloud compute. Sandboxes are not required by the rules. The track text "agents that write, run, and test code in Token Factory" is on the Devpost overview page.
- **SWE-agent angle:** 7,000+ SWE-bench and SWE-rebench environments come preloaded (https://docs.tokenfactory.nebius.com/sandboxes/swe-agents). A Dockerfile build is available through `contree build`.
- **Fallback if access is not granted:** run tests in a Nebius Serverless Job (section 3), or in another sandbox outside Nebius.

## 3. Serverless Jobs and Endpoints (AI Cloud)

Sources: https://docs.nebius.com/serverless/overview, .../quickstart/jobs, .../quickstart/endpoints, .../lifecycle, .../pricing-quotas.

- **Jobs:** run a container to completion, with no public URL. They cannot be stopped or restarted. The disk is wiped at the end. Logs are viewable through the web console and CLI only, not the REST API. Billing is per second.
- **Endpoints:** a container serving HTTP on a managed HTTPS URL, which can be stopped and started. Billing is per second, and nothing is charged while stopped. Token auth is optional.
- **Job CLI (docs example):**
```
nebius ai create --type job --name my-job --image <img> --container-command bash --args "-c '...'" --platform gpu-l40s-a --preset 1gpu-8vcpu-32gb --timeout 1h
```
  Logs and status come from `nebius ai job get-by-name` and related commands. I did not check whether the `--args` quoting works for a multi-command string, so test it.
- **Endpoint CLI (docs example):**
```
nebius ai endpoint create --name x --image nginx:alpine --platform cpu-d3 --preset 4vcpu-16gb --public --container-port 80 --auth token --token "$T" --subnet-id <id>
```
  Other flags documented: `--env k=v`, `--env-secret`, `--registry-username/--registry-password`, and `--volume`.
- **CPU-only:** yes. The endpoint example uses `cpu-d3` with `4vcpu-16gb`. Jobs on CPU platforms are UNVERIFIED, because the job quickstart only shows a GPU example.
- **Pricing:** there is no separate serverless price. It uses Compute VM pricing. Non-GPU AMD Epyc Genoa is $0.015 per CPU-hour and $0.0045 per GiB-hour of RAM, until the Oct 1, 2026 change. After that I could not tell which rate applies, so verify on https://docs.nebius.com/compute/resources/pricing.
- **Cold start:** the docs give no figure. Statuses go `PROVISIONING`, `STARTING`, `IMAGE_PULLING`, `RUNNING`. If capacity is unavailable, it retries for up to 30 minutes, then ends in an `ERROR` status. Image pull time depends on your image size.
- **Quotas:** you need at least one VM available under Compute quotas, plus a VPC allocation for endpoints. Check the Quotas page in the console first.
- **Node or Python app on an endpoint:** reasonable. Any container with a listening port gets an HTTPS URL, and it accepts env vars, secrets and private registries. Ship a normal Dockerfile.
- **`npm install && npm test` in a Job:** feasible in principle, since the container command is arbitrary. The repo must be cloned inside the container, and outbound network access from jobs is not documented. UNVERIFIED. It also takes minutes per run, so Sandboxes are better for tight loops.
- **Hackathon note:** the rules list Serverless Jobs, Serverless Endpoints and DevPods as qualifying Nebius AI Cloud compute.

## 4. Tavily

Sources: https://docs.tavily.com/llms.txt, and the pages under /documentation/api-reference/endpoint/.

- **SDKs:** Python `pip install tavily-python`, with `TavilyClient(api_key=...)`, `.search(...)` and `.extract(...)`. JavaScript `npm i @tavily/core`. There is also a `tavily-cli` (`tvly search`, `tvly extract`, `tvly crawl`, `tvly research`) and a remote MCP server at `https://mcp.tavily.com/mcp/`.
- **REST:** base `https://api.tavily.com`. The `POST /search` body has `query`, `search_depth` (`basic` | `advanced` | `fast` | `ultra-fast`), `max_results` (0-20, default 10) and `include_raw_content` (bool, `"markdown"` or `"text"`).
