tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

schema.name: Workflow
schema.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: mcp__gmail__draft_gmail_message
tools.description:
Creates a draft email in the user's Gmail account. Supports new, reply, and forward
drafts with optional attachments. Supports Gmail's "Send As" feature to draft from
configured alias addresses.

To save a forward as a draft for review, pass forward_message_id. The original
subject, body (quoted with a "Forwarded message" header), and attachments are
carried over. In forward mode, body (if any) is prepended as a note, subject is
optional, and threading, reply, and signature options do not apply.

SCHEDULED SEND IS NOT AVAILABLE. Gmail's REST API exposes no send-time
parameter; the Schedule send feature is web-UI only, and a message cannot be
placed in the Scheduled folder through the API. Do not claim a message was
scheduled. To deliver at a chosen time, create a draft with
draft_gmail_message. An external scheduler must retain the message data to
create and send a new message via send_gmail_message then, or call
users.drafts.send with the draft ID returned by draft_gmail_message.
Alternatively, let the user schedule the draft in the Gmail UI.

schema.name: mcp__gmail__draft_gmail_message
schema.description:
Creates a draft email in the user's Gmail account. Supports new, reply, and forward
drafts with optional attachments. Supports Gmail's "Send As" feature to draft from
configured alias addresses.

To save a forward as a draft for review, pass forward_message_id. The original
subject, body (quoted with a "Forwarded message" header), and attachments are
carried over. In forward mode, body (if any) is prepended as a note, subject is
optional, and threading, reply, and signature options do not apply.

SCHEDULED SEND IS NOT AVAILABLE. Gmail's REST API exposes no send-time
parameter; the Schedule send feature is web-UI only, and a message cannot be
placed in the Scheduled folder through the API. Do not claim a message was
scheduled. To deliver at a chosen time, create a draft with
draft_gmail_message. An external scheduler must retain the message data to
create and send a new message via send_gmail_message then, or call
users.drafts.send with the draft ID returned by draft_gmail_message.
Alternatively, let the user schedule the draft in the Gmail UI.

user_google_email.description: The user's Google email address. Required for authentication.

subject.description: Email subject. Required unless forwarding (then defaults to 'Fwd: <original subject>').

body.description: Email body. Required unless forwarding, where it becomes an optional note prepended above the quoted original.

body_format.description: Email body format. Use 'plain' for plaintext or 'html' for HTML content.

forward_message_id.description: Set to a Gmail message ID to save a forward of that message as a draft for review. The original subject, body, and (optionally) attachments are carried over; 'body' becomes an optional note prepended to the forward.

include_forwarded_attachments.description: When forwarding, whether to include the original message's attachments. Ignored unless forward_message_id is set.

from_name.description: Optional sender display name (e.g., 'Peter Hartree'). If provided, the From header will be formatted as 'Name <email>'.

from_email.description: Optional 'Send As' alias email address. Must be configured in Gmail settings (Settings > Accounts > Send mail as). If not provided, uses the account's default Send As address, falling back to the authenticated user's email when Gmail returns no usable Send-As entry or settings access is not authorized.

thread_id.description: Optional Gmail thread ID to reply within. When in_reply_to is omitted, replies to the latest non-draft, non-trash message with an RFC Message-ID.

in_reply_to.description: Optional RFC Message-ID to explicitly reply to a specific message (e.g., '<message123@gmail.com>'). Omit to reply to the latest eligible message in thread_id.

references.description: Optional Message-ID ancestry chain. Normally omit when thread_id is provided; the server derives the chain through the selected reply target.

attachments.description: Optional list of attachments. Each can have: 'url' (fetch from URL — works with MCP attachment URLs from get_drive_file_download_url / get_gmail_attachment_content), OR 'path' (file path, auto-encodes), OR 'content' (standard base64, not urlsafe) + 'filename'. Optional 'mime_type'. Optional 'content_id' (string) makes the attachment inline-rendered: it lands in a multipart/related part with `Content-ID: ` and `Content-Disposition: inline`, and the HTML body can reference it via `` (RFC 2392). Without `content_id` the attachment is a regular multipart/mixed attachment.

include_signature.description: Whether to append the Gmail signature from Settings > Signature when available. Defaults to true.

quote_original.description: Whether to include the original message as a quoted reply. Only has an effect when thread_id is provided. Defaults to false.

tools.name: mcp__gmail__get_gmail_attachment_content

schema.name: mcp__gmail__get_gmail_attachment_content
schema.description:
Downloads an email attachment and saves it to local disk.

In stdio mode, returns the local file path for direct access.
In HTTP mode, returns a temporary download URL (valid for 1 hour).
May re-fetch message metadata to resolve filename and MIME type.

message_id.description: The ID of the Gmail message containing the attachment.

attachment_id.description: The ID of the attachment to download.

user_google_email.description: The user's Google email address. Required.

return_base64.description:
When True, includes the full attachment as a
standard base64 string in the response (in addition to any file
path or download URL). Useful for sandboxed clients that cannot
reach localhost download URLs or the MCP server's local file
paths (e.g. containerized agents with network allowlists). The
returned base64 uses the standard alphabet, so it can be passed
directly to tools like ``draft_gmail_message`` that expect
standard (not URL-safe) base64. Default False preserves the
existing behavior and response size.

attachment_index.description:
Zero-based attachment position from
the message-content response. Lets the server resolve Gmail's
refreshed attachment IDs against current metadata before every
download, selecting the current attachment ID, filename and MIME type.

tools.name: mcp__gmail__get_gmail_message_content
tools.description:
Retrieves the full content (subject, sender, recipients, body) of a specific Gmail message.

Bodies are returned inline and truncated at 20,000 characters. Set full=True to
get the complete, untruncated message instead: it is exported to storage and the
response carries a short-lived download URL (HTTP transport) or file path (stdio
transport) rather than the body, so large messages never stream through the model
context. Stateless deployments without GCS staging have no storage, so there
full=True returns the untruncated body inline; with GCS staging configured it
returns a signed download URL like any other HTTP deployment.

schema.name: mcp__gmail__get_gmail_message_content
schema.description:
Retrieves the full content (subject, sender, recipients, body) of a specific Gmail message.

Bodies are returned inline and truncated at 20,000 characters. Set full=True to
get the complete, untruncated message instead: it is exported to storage and the
response carries a short-lived download URL (HTTP transport) or file path (stdio
transport) rather than the body, so large messages never stream through the model

Use for messages large enough to hit the truncation limit, or when byte-exact fidelity is needed (pair with body_format='raw' for a .eml export).

tools.name: mcp__gmail__manage_gmail_filter
tools.description:
Manages Gmail filters: create, delete, update, and apply to existing mail.

- update: Gmail has no filter update API, so the filter is recreated (new
  one first, then the old one is deleted) and its ID changes. A passed
  criteria or filter_action replaces that whole object; omit one to keep
  the old filter's.
- apply: runs a filter's label actions on mail ALREADY in the mailbox
  (Gmail filters only act on new mail). Only matching messages change,
  not whole conversations as in the web UI. Use filter_id, or criteria +
  filter_action for an ad-hoc run. Forwarding is never applied. Use
  dry_run=true first to see the search query and the match count.
  Needs the gmail.modify scope in addition to gmail.settings.basic.

- apply: runs a filter's label actions on mail ALREADY in the mailbox

tools.name: mcp__gmail__send_gmail_message
tools.description:
Sends an email using the user's Gmail account. Supports new emails, replies, and
forwards, with optional attachments. Supports Gmail's "Send As" feature to send
from configured alias addresses.

To forward an existing message, pass forward_message_id. The original subject,
body (quoted with a "Forwarded message" header), and attachments are carried over.
In forward mode, body (if any) is prepended as a note and subject is optional.
Threading, reply, and signature options do not apply when forwarding.

THIS TOOL SENDS IMMEDIATELY AND CANNOT SCHEDULE. Gmail's REST API exposes no
send-time parameter; Schedule send is a web-UI feature with no API equivalent,
so no argument to this tool can defer delivery. Never tell a user a message
was scheduled. For "prepare now, deliver later", create a draft with
draft_gmail_message. An external scheduler must retain the message data to
create and send a new message via send_gmail_message at the chosen time, or
call users.drafts.send with the draft ID returned by draft_gmail_message.
Alternatively, let the user schedule that draft in the Gmail UI.

schema.name: mcp__gmail__send_gmail_message
schema.description:
Sends an email using the user's Gmail account. Supports new emails, replies, and
forwards, with optional attachments. Supports Gmail's "Send As" feature to send
from configured alias addresses.

To forward an existing message, pass forward_message_id. The original subject,
body (quoted with a "Forwarded message" header), and attachments are carried over.
In forward mode, body (if any) is prepended as a note and subject is optional.
Threading, reply, and signature options do not apply when forwarding.

THIS TOOL SENDS IMMEDIATELY AND CANNOT SCHEDULE. Gmail's REST API exposes no
send-time parameter; Schedule send is a web-UI feature with no API equivalent,
so no argument to this tool can defer delivery. Never tell a user a message
was scheduled. For "prepare now, deliver later", create a draft with
draft_gmail_message. An external scheduler must retain the message data to
create and send a new message via send_gmail_message at the chosen time, or
call users.drafts.send with the draft ID returned by draft_gmail_message.
Alternatively, let the user schedule that draft in the Gmail UI.

user_google_email.description: The user's Google email address. Required for authentication.

to.description: Recipient email address. Optional when replying with reply_all=True, which derives it from the thread.

subject.description: Email subject. Required when sending; optional when forwarding (defaults to 'Fwd: <original subject>').

body.description: Email body content (plain text or HTML). Required when sending. When forwarding, this is an optional note prepended above the quoted original.

body_format.description: Format of the body content (and of the prepended note when forwarding). Use 'plain' for plaintext or 'html' for HTML content.

forward_message_id.description: Set to a Gmail message ID to forward that message instead of composing a new one. The original subject, body, and (optionally) attachments are carried over; 'body' becomes an optional note prepended to the forward.

include_forwarded_attachments.description: When forwarding, whether to include the original message's attachments. Ignored unless forward_message_id is set.

from_name.description: Optional sender display name (e.g., 'Peter Hartree'). If provided, the From header will be formatted as 'Name <email>'.

from_email.description: Optional 'Send As' alias email address. Must be configured in Gmail settings (Settings > Accounts > Send mail as). If not provided, uses the authenticated user's email.

thread_id.description: Optional Gmail thread ID to reply within. When in_reply_to is omitted, replies to the latest non-draft, non-trash message with an RFC Message-ID.

in_reply_to.description: Optional RFC Message-ID to explicitly reply to a specific message (e.g., '<message123@gmail.com>'). Omit to reply to the latest eligible message in thread_id.

references.description: Optional Message-ID ancestry chain. Normally omit when thread_id is provided; the server derives the chain through the selected reply target.

attachments.description: Optional list of attachments. Each can have: "url" (fetch from URL — works with MCP attachment URLs from get_drive_file_download_url / get_gmail_attachment_content), OR "path" (file path, auto-encodes), OR "content" (standard base64, not urlsafe) + "filename". Optional "mime_type". Optional "content_id" (string) makes the attachment inline-rendered: it lands in a multipart/related part with `Content-ID: ` and `Content-Disposition: inline`, and the HTML body can reference it via `` (RFC 2392). Without `content_id` the attachment is a regular multipart/mixed attachment. Example: [{"url": "https://host/attachments/abc-123", "filename": "report.pdf"}]

include_signature.description: Whether to append the Gmail signature from Settings > Signature when available. Defaults to true.

quote_original.description: Whether to include the message being replied to as a quoted original. Only has an effect when thread_id is provided. Defaults to false.

reply_all.description: Whether to derive reply-all recipients from the thread: To = the sender being replied to, Cc = the other participants, excluding the authenticated account and from_email. Requires thread_id. Explicit to/cc win; when cc is omitted the sender being replied to is added to the derived Cc if they are not already in To. Defaults to false.

tools.name: mcp__gmail__start_google_auth
tools.description:
Manually initiate Google OAuth authentication flow.

NOTE: This is a legacy OAuth 2.0 tool and is disabled when OAuth 2.1 is enabled.
The authentication system automatically handles credential checks and prompts for
authentication when needed. Only use this tool if:
1. You need to re-authenticate with different credentials
2. You want to proactively authenticate before using other tools
3. The automatic authentication flow failed and you need to retry

In most cases, simply try calling the Google Workspace tool you need - it will
automatically handle authentication if required.

"""Pre-render the read-only API into web/dist for the static demo (GitHub Pages).

  cd web && VITE_STATIC=1 npx vite build --base /greenlight/ && cd ..
  python scripts/build_static.py

Writes the same JSON the FastAPI server returns (server/app.py) for health, replays, the official
scoreboard and the eval cases, plus a 404.html copy of index.html so deep links like
/greenlight/replay/<id> load the app. Stdlib only, so CI needs no project install.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import shutil
import sys
import tomllib
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
DIST = ROOT / "web" / "dist"
REPLAYS = ROOT / "replays"
BOARD = ROOT / "evals" / "results" / "eval-official" / "scoreboard.json"
DATASET = ROOT / "evals" / "dataset.toml"


def _events(path: Path) -> list[dict]:
    return [json.loads(ln) for ln in path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines() if ln.strip()]


def _meta(path: Path, events: list[dict]) -> dict:
    run = next((e for e in events if e["type"] == "run"), {})
    res = next((e for e in reversed(events) if e["type"] == "result"), {})
    return {
        "id": path.stem, "lib": run.get("lib"), "to_major": run.get("to_major"),
        "source": run.get("source"), "ref": run.get("ref"),
        "status": res.get("status"), "headline": res.get("headline"),
        "from_version": res.get("from_version"), "to_version": res.get("to_version"),
        "usd": res.get("usd"), "seconds": res.get("seconds"), "events": len(events),
    }


def _write(rel: str, data: object) -> None:
    out = DIST / "api" / f"{rel}.json"
    out.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    out.write_text(json.dumps(data, ensure_ascii=False), encoding="utf-8")


def main() -> int:
    if not (DIST / "index.html").exists():
        print("web/dist is missing: build the web app first", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    metas = []
    for path in sorted(REPLAYS.glob("*.jsonl")):
        events = _events(path)
        metas.append(_meta(path, events))
        _write(f"replays/{path.stem}", events)
    _write("replays", metas)
    _write("scoreboard", json.loads(BOARD.read_text(encoding="utf-8")) if BOARD.exists() else {"cases": 0, "rows": []})
    cases = tomllib.loads(DATASET.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))["case"]
    _write("cases", [{k: c.get(k) for k in ("id", "repo", "sha", "lib", "to")} for c in cases])
    _write("health", {"ok": True, "live": False, "executor": "docker", "spent_usd": 0, "replays": len(metas)})
    shutil.copyfile(DIST / "index.html", DIST / "404.html")
    (DIST / ".nojekyll").touch()
    print(f"static API written: {len(metas)} replays")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

# Static demo on GitHub Pages: the web app plus pre-rendered replays and scoreboard (no server, no keys).
name: Deploy demo to GitHub Pages

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

concurrency:
  group: pages
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: npm
          cache-dependency-path: web/package-lock.json
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - name: Build web app (static mode)
        working-directory: web
        env:
          VITE_STATIC: "1"
        run: |
          npm ci
          npx tsc -b
          npx vite build --base "/${{ github.event.repository.name }}/"
      - name: Pre-render API
        run: python scripts/build_static.py
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with:
          path: web/dist
      - id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4
EOF

lines: -**The breaking dependency upgrades that Dependabot can't do.**

-Greenlight reads the official migration guide, rewrites your code for the new major version, and runs your own test suite in a sandbox until it passes. Then it proves the result wasn't faked, and opens a PR that cites a source for every change.
-All of it runs on **NVIDIA Nemotron models served by Nebius Token Factory**, with **Tavily** for research.
-> Built for the [Nebius × NVIDIA Global AI Hackathon](https://nebiusglobalaihackathon.devpost.com/), Coding & Agentic Engineering track. MIT licensed.
-  ✓ research  348 rules from the official migration guide (Tavily → Nemotron 3.5 Lightning)
-  ✓ migrate   3 files rewritten in parallel (Nemotron 3 Super)
-  ■ GREEN     pydantic 1.10.13 → 2.14.0 · all anti-cheat checks pass · $0.04 · 64s

-Version-bump bots open the PR and stop there. Major upgrades such as pydantic 1→2, numpy 1→2, pandas 1→2 and SQLAlchemy 1.4→2.0 break the code, so those PRs sit red for months. Teams stay on unsupported versions and pile up security debt.
-Fixing one is tedious but well specified:
-That's exactly the loop an agent should run, as long as you can **trust** the result.
-| **Baseline** | Clone at a pinned commit into an isolated sandbox, install (including Poetry/Hatch/PEP 735 dev dependencies), run the tests. The passing set is the contract. | none |
-| **Bump** | Rewrite the version pin in every manifest (requirements, `setup.py`, `setup.cfg`, `pyproject`/Poetry), reinstall, rerun the tests. Now they're red. | none |

-| **Research** | Tavily searches the library's official docs and extracts the migration guide. Lightning turns it into a **rule sheet** of old API → new API, each rule with a grep pattern and a source URL. Rules not grounded in the source text are dropped. The sheet is cached. | Nemotron 3.5 Lightning |
-| **Plan** | Ultra gets the grouped failures plus every call site the rules match, and writes a structured plan: files, rule ids, dependency changes and risks. | Nemotron 3 Ultra (reasoning on) |
-| **Migrate** | Super rewrites each planned file in one pass, **in parallel**. Each rewrite is syntax-checked and size-checked before it's written. | Nemotron 3 Super |

-| **Repair** | A tool loop (`read_file`, `grep`, `apply_patch`, `rewrite_file`, `run_tests`, `search_docs`, `reinstall`) fixes whatever still fails. When progress stalls, **Ultra re-plans** from the current diff. | Super, plus Ultra on escalation |
-| **Verify** | Anti-cheat checks against the real sandbox state (below). | none |
-| **PR** | A PR description with a change table that cites the migration-guide rule behind each edit. | Nemotron 3.5 Lightning |
-### Trust: a green suite only counts if it was earned

-Agents under pressure delete tests, skip them, pin the old version back, or hide errors. Greenlight enforces these rules **in the tool layer**, and verifies them afterwards from the sandbox, not from what the model claims:
-- every test that passed at baseline still passes
-- the target major version is actually installed
-- the upgrade pin is still in the manifests (rolling it back is refused at edit time)
-- tests are the contract: a test file may be edited only to follow a renamed/moved API it uses directly
-  (e.g. `from pydantic import BaseSettings`). Every assertion, `pytest.raises`, test function and marker
-  must survive (an edit that deletes or weakens one is refused at edit time and re-audited from git)
-- no module named after the library (a fake `pydantic.py` that hijacks the import is refused)
-- the test count didn't drop, and no test is newly skipped
-The tool layer also refuses repeated identical calls, which stops the loops agents fall into.
-### Cost safety: it can't run up your bill

-Token Factory is postpaid, so we built a **hard budget guard**. Every call's worst-case cost is reserved *before* it's sent, priced from the live per-token rates. Calls that would cross the global, daily or per-run cap are refused.
-- a torn line after a power cut counts *as spend*
-- an unsettled reservation counts at its worst case
-So a crash can only make the guard stricter. Run `greenlight budget` to see spend against the caps.
-## How we use NVIDIA Nemotron on Nebius Token Factory
-We route each job to the cheapest model that does it well. Every call goes through one OpenAI-compatible client pointed at `https://api.tokenfactory.nebius.com/v1/`:
-| `nvidia/Nemotron-3-Ultra-550b-a55b` | Planner, and re-planner when stuck | Best reasoning, called 1–3× per run, with reasoning on |
-| `nvidia/nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b` | Code editor (bulk migration plus tool loop) | Reliable tool calling and idiomatic code at about a third of Ultra's price |
-| `nvidia/Nemotron-3_5-Lightning` | Turns migration guides into rule sheets, writes PR text | $0.06/$0.24 per 1M tokens at ~300 tok/s, ideal for long-document extraction |
-- Reasoning is turned on per role (`chat_template_kwargs.enable_thinking`).
-- Every call is logged with tokens, $ and latency, and shown live in the UI's routing panel.
-- One API key gave us every Nemotron tier, so we could move each role between models with a one-line change.
-- Ultra's speed (~520 tok/s) made reasoning-heavy planning cheap enough to run on every upgrade.

- quick-regeneration: Regenerates one existing localized episode group (by group ID or nearby timeline mark) as a single audio-only ElevenLabs retake, reusing the group's latest approved payload, voice, model and language, and returns one MP3. Use when asked to retake, redo or quickly regenerate one clip or group of an already-dubbed episode. Not for full dubs, combined audio, Resolve edits, or QA/bookmark work (use reviewer-correction).
- reviewer-correction: Applies reviewer or QA corrections to an existing localized dub: reconciles reviewer findings, regenerates or places corrected audio, adds Resolve bookmarks, and delivers a verified paste-ready Resolve handoff without mutating existing content. Use when given reviewer CSVs, QA findings or round-based feedback on a dubbed episode. Use quick-regeneration for one standalone retake with no QA or Resolve work; not for visual review or for creating a new dub.
- security-best-practices: Language and framework specific security best-practice reviews, secure-by-default coding guidance and prioritized vulnerability reports for Python (Django, FastAPI, Flask), JavaScript/TypeScript (Express, Next.js, React, Vue, jQuery, general frontend) and Go backends. Use only when the user explicitly asks for security best practices, a security review or report, or secure-by-default help in those languages. Not for general code review, debugging or non-security tasks.
- security-threat-model: Repository-grounded threat modeling: enumerates trust boundaries, assets, attacker capabilities, abuse paths and mitigations, and writes a concise Markdown threat model file with a Mermaid diagram. Use only when the user explicitly asks to threat model a codebase or path, enumerate threats or abuse paths, or do AppSec threat modeling. Not for architecture summaries, general code review or non-security design work.
- speaker-aware-dubbing: Builds review-ready speaker-aware localized dubs from verified media when speaker identity is not authoritative in the supplied files: WhisperX diarization plus acoustic and targeted visual evidence, translation alignment, approved voice casting, compact sentence-aware ElevenLabs groups, natural tails, and a compact one-row Resolve handoff of separate clips (never a combined mix). Use for a new dub, speaker tagging, or voice casting. Use translation-dubbing when SRT speaker labels are authoritative, quick-regeneration for one-group retakes, reviewer-correction for existing-dub repairs.
- sushi-infotik-carousel: Creates or audits Sushi x InfoTik Instagram carousels: six 1080x1350 4:5 slides with the locked original 2D orange octopus mascot, locked caption typography, split-scene structure, bottom safe area and Drive handoff. Use for work in E:/ai/claude/carousel/sushi-imagegen-pipeline. Not for Orano carousels.
- translation-dubbing: Builds review-ready regular localized dubs from verified source media and a supplied speaker-labeled SRT: trusts the supplied labels and frozen voice map, translates and aligns text, generates natural-tail grouped ElevenLabs takes, packs separate clips onto one Resolve row, and never creates a combined mix. Use when asked to dub or translate an episode that already has speaker labels. Use speaker-aware-dubbing when identity is missing, quick-regeneration for one-group retakes, reviewer-correction for existing-dub repairs.
- ugc: One-shot pipeline: takes silent UGC video clips, scores them with a rotating track from a curated commercially-safe music library, writes human-sounding platform-specific captions that always mention the Infotik app by name and link infotik.co, and posts them straight to the named social channels (TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, etc.) via Buffer — no separate steps, no stopping to ask which distribution method. Use this skill whenever the user says something like 'compile the UGC videos and post to TikTok/IG', 'process the new videos and put them up', or otherwise asks to take raw clips all the way to posted. Trigger even on short requests like 'post the new videos' in the context of Infotik's UGC content pipeline.
- workspace-memory: Look up context about any project on E:\ai or D:\ from the shared workspace memory — the Obsidian Knowledge-Vault, MEMORY-HUB.md project registry, mirrored agent memories, and the graphify code/doc graph of every project. Use when you need to know what a project is, where its code/docs/memory live, how a symbol or feature works across repos, which projects are related, or what past sessions decided — and the answer isn't already in the current repo's AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md. Not needed for routine edits inside a project you already understand.
- x-engagement-post-generator: Researches timely AI conversations and drafts high-conversation, conversion-aware X posts for Orano AI (@oranoai) or Manu Parasuraman (@ParasuramanManu), with Buffer-only publishing and logging. Use when drafting, revising or scheduling an X post or tweet where the goal is meaningful replies, reach or qualified clicks.
- background: Run a command or agent in the background (non-blocking)
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings up to many, some of them uncertain); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- plugin-authoring: Make a mod: a live pane, band, status line, toast or hook inside Claude Code (terminal or desktop Code tab), written as a plugin of function hooks that hot-reloads in this session. Load before writing or debugging a hooks module.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

Code generation is solved. What happens next is the challenge.

Life After Code is the GitLab Transcend Hackathon. �WHY JOIN?

Use agents,flows, triggers, and MCP servers - as many features of the GitLab Duo Agent Platform and see how much of your software development lifecycle you can automate.

Compete for $45,000 in cash.

REQUIREMENTS
WHAT TO BUILD

Pick one Path. Then build a project that fits one of three levels of autonomy.

Every project must use GitLab Duo Agent Platform features, such as agents, flows, or MCP clients.�

Path A: Start Fresh
Build a new AI-powered project on GitLab that shows agentic automation of the post-code lifecycle. You create the app, the CI/CD pipeline, and the automation from scratch. Your project must be new work, created for this hackathon. Deployment is optional. Deploy on Google Cloud to be eligible for up to 0.2 bonus points.

Path B: Bring Your Own
Take an existing MIT-licensed open-source project. It can be yours or a fork. Import it to GitLab, build the AI-powered post-code automation around it, and deploy it. You must build the automation and deploy the project on or after October 5th. Deploy anywhere. Deploy on Google Cloud to be eligible for up to 0.2 bonus points. Read the Official Rules for details.

�

Choose your level of autonomy

Assisted: You approve every step. Your agents and flows propose actions and wait for your go-ahead before they proceed. You stay in the loop at every stage.

Example: An agent reviews your MR and flags a security vulnerability. It suggests a fix and waits for you to approve before committing. Then it runs the pipeline and waits for you to approve the deployment.

Supervised: You approve the outcome, not the individual steps. Your agents execute a multi-step workflow on their own, clearing gates and making decisions along the way. You review the end result, not every individual action.

Example: You push code. Agents handle code review, fix a failing pipeline, remediate a security finding, and deploy to staging. You get a summary and approve the production deployment.

Hands-off: You set the intent and walk away. A full loop from code to production with no human in the middle. You push code or create an issue, and the next time you check in, it's live.

Example: You create an issue. Agents review it, create 1+ MRs, run security scans, fix what they find, merge when everything passes, deploy to staging, validate, promote to production, and post a summary on the original issue. You touched nothing.

**The examples above are here to get you thinking. We expect submissions that go well beyond them.

Prizes for every level of autonomy.�

�

This is the heart of the challenge. Build automation that reaches across GitLab�s DevSecOps lifecycle, not just one corner of it. There are nine stages:

plan � create � verify � package � secure � release � configure � monitor � govern

You do not have to use every feature inside a stage. Touching the stage counts.

Prizes for the Most Stages Covered�

�

Deployment is only a requirement for Path B. Deploy anywhere you like. Google Cloud is not required for either Path.

If you deploy on Google Cloud, your project is eligible for up to 0.2 bonus points. We add these points once, after judges score your project. The highest possible final score is 5.2.

To be eligible, you must:

Include your Google Cloud deployment code in your public GitLab repository.

Provide a link to your live project on Google Cloud. It must be public and available to judges.

See Resources Tab for how to get started on Google Cloud. Read the Official Rules for details.

Your project, built with the required technologies.

�WHY JOIN?

Use agents,flows, triggers, and MCP servers - as many features of the GitLab Duo Agent Platform and see how much of your software development lifecycle you can automate.

Compete for $45,000 in cash.

Get your work in front of judges from GitLab, Google, and Anthropic.

Pick one Path. Then build a project that fits one of three levels of autonomy.

Every project must use GitLab Duo Agent Platform features, such as agents, flows, or MCP clients.�

Path A: Start Fresh
Build a new AI-powered project on GitLab that shows agentic automation of the post-code lifecycle. You create the app, the CI/CD pipeline, and the automation from scratch. Your project must be new work, created for this hackathon. Deployment is optional. Deploy on Google Cloud to be eligible for up to 0.2 bonus points.

Path B: Bring Your Own
Take an existing MIT-licensed open-source project. It can be yours or a fork. Import it to GitLab, build the AI-powered post-code automation around it, and deploy it. You must build the automation and deploy the project on or after October 5th. Deploy anywhere. Deploy on Google Cloud to be eligible for up to 0.2 bonus points. Read the Official Rules for details.

�

Choose your level of autonomy

Assisted: You approve every step. Your agents and flows propose actions and wait for your go-ahead before they proceed. You stay in the loop at every stage.

Example: An agent reviews your MR and flags a security vulnerability. It suggests a fix and waits for you to approve before committing. Then it runs the pipeline and waits for you to approve the deployment.

Supervised: You approve the outcome, not the individual steps. Your agents execute a multi-step workflow on their own, clearing gates and making decisions along the way. You review the end result, not every individual action.

Example: You push code. Agents handle code review, fix a failing pipeline, remediate a security finding, and deploy to staging. You get a summary and approve the production deployment.

Hands-off: You set the intent and walk away. A full loop from code to production with no human in the middle. You push code or create an issue, and the next time you check in, it's live.

Example: You create an issue. Agents review it, create 1+ MRs, run security scans, fix what they find, merge when everything passes, deploy to staging, validate, promote to production, and post a summary on the original issue. You touched nothing.

plan � create � verify � package � secure � release � configure � monitor � govern
